content: The conifers, classified under the division Pinophyta (also known as Coniferae), are cone-bearing seed plants with vascular tissue. All living conifers are woody plants, with most being trees and a few being shrubs. Examples of conifers include cedars, pines, firs, spruces, redwoods, junipers, and yews. These plants are found naturally in almost all parts of the world and often dominate their habitats, such as in the taiga biome. Conifers are of significant economic importance, particularly for timber and paper production, with their wood commonly referred to as softwood. There are approximately 630 living species of conifers. The earliest conifers appeared during the late Carboniferous period, around 300 million years ago. The division name Pinophyta adheres to the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN) rules, which allow names to be derived from an included family, in this case, Pinaceae (the pine family), or to be descriptive. Older names like Coniferophyta and Coniferales are no longer valid. Conifers are often equated with gymnosperms, but they represent only one of the four groups within gymnosperms. The division Pinophyta contains a single class, Pinopsida, which includes both living and fossil taxa. While some taxonomists have proposed subdividing living conifers into multiple orders, the majority of experts prefer to classify all families within a single order, Pinales. Conifers are currently recognized as comprising six to eight families, 65-70 genera, and 600-630 species. Conifers are an ancient group with a fossil record extending back to the late Carboniferous period. Fossil evidence shows that many modern genera were already recognizable 60-120 million years ago. Extinct conifer-like plants, such as Cordaitales and Voltziales, were diverse and included forms distinct from modern conifers, such as herbaceous species without woody stems. All living conifers are woody plants, with most exhibiting monopodial growth (a single, straight trunk with side branches). Mature conifers vary greatly in size, from less than one meter to over 100 meters in height. The tallest living tree is a Coast Redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) at 115.2 meters, while the largest by volume is a Giant Sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) at 1,486.9 cubic meters. The thickest trunk belongs to a Montezuma Cypress (Taxodium mucronatum) with a diameter of 11.42 meters, and the oldest known conifer is a Great Basin Bristlecone Pine (Pinus longaeva) at 4,700 years old. The foliage of conifers varies widely. Many species have long, thin, needle-like leaves, while others, such as those in the Cupressaceae and Podocarpaceae families, have flat, scale-like leaves. Some genera, like Agathis and Nageia, have broad, strap-shaped leaves. Leaf arrangement is typically spiral, but some species exhibit opposite pairs or whorls. Leaf size ranges from 2 mm in scale-leaved species to 400 mm in some pines. Stomata are present on the leaves and can close during dry or cold conditions. Most conifers have dark green leaves to maximize energy absorption in low-light environments, though some species in sunny regions have yellow-green or glaucous leaves. The majority of conifers are evergreen, retaining their leaves for 2-40 years, but a few genera, such as Larix and Metasequoia, are deciduous. Conifers reproduce through cones, which are specialized structures for seed development. Most conifers are monoecious, with both male and female cones on the same plant, though some are dioecious. Male cones produce pollen, which is wind-dispersed to female cones. Fertilization occurs when pollen reaches the female gametophyte, leading to the development of a seed. Cones vary in size and structure, with some being woody and others fleshy. Seeds are dispersed by wind, birds, or other animals, depending on the species. In some fire-adapted pines, seeds are stored in closed cones for decades and released only after a fire. The life cycle of conifers begins with the release of pollen from male cones, which fertilizes the ovum in female cones. The resulting zygote develops into an embryo, which, along with surrounding integument cells, forms a seed. The seed eventually falls to the ground, germinates, and grows into a mature plant that produces cones, completing the cycle. Despite their relatively small number of species, conifers play a crucial ecological role. They dominate vast areas of land, particularly in boreal forests of the northern hemisphere and mountainous regions in cooler climates. Many conifers produce resin, which protects against insects and fungal infections. Fossilized resin, known as amber, is a valuable material.
